answer: Use the clock command. Set the zone with 'set clock timezone <value>', for example 'set clock timezone Beijing-Chongqing-Hong_Kong-Urumqi[GMT+08:00]'. The value list runs from International Date Line West[GMT-12:00] through Kiritimati[GMT+14:00]; the default is Universal-Time-Coordinated. To see where the node gets its time, read the time-source attribute: 'show clock time-source' returns ntp (the NE uses NTP for synchronization) or manual (the NE uses its own internal clock); the default is manual. 'show clock' also returns current-time, universal-time, timezone, uptime, uptime-seconds, DST-active (true/false, default false) and last-time-jump, which reports '<time1> to <time2>' and ignores jumps of less than 10 seconds. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. If DNS is not properly configured, show clock can take up to 2 minutes to respond.

Yes. 'set ne node-type OADM' converts it. node-type takes ILA, OADM or XPDR; it can only be set/changed on a 1830 GX G34c chassis, which defaults to ILA. G31/G32 chassis support only OADM, G42 defaults to XPDR. Beginning with R7.0 the G34c supports OADM node-type. Pre-conditions to configure node-type OADM: no OMS monitoring-mode in the system may be 'ila-with-equalization' or 'not-monitored', that is no spectrum (or ochm) objects exist, and no direction-* may exist. Going the other way, to configure ILA: no OMS monitoring-mode on the dwdm-line ports may be 'intrusive' (no RD or PAx card can exist), and no degree, no oxcon and no nmc may exist. Note that G34c SLTE mode (l0-mode-op slte) is supported only when node-type is ILA, not with OADM.

'show ne-function' lists the NE generic functions in one place. It is a show-only command with no parameters, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The output enumerates the node's directions and amplifier objects together, for example on a 1830 GX G30 node: direction-1 through direction-8, amplifier-raman-1-7, amplifier-1-1-A, amplifier-1-1-B, amplifier-1-3.1-drop, amplifier-1-5-A, amplifier-1-5-B, amplifier-2-1-A, amplifier-2-1-B, amplifier-2-3-A, amplifier-2-3-B, and the ne-function entry itself.

Use 'set ntp ntp-enabled true ntp-auth-enabled true'. ntp-enabled takes true/false and defaults to true; ntp-auth-enabled takes true/false and defaults to false, so authentication must be turned on explicitly. The ntp object also carries assignment-method (manual, dhcp or both, default both), which selects whether the system uses manually configured values, DHCP-supplied values, or both. 'show ntp [ntp-enabled] [ntp-auth-enabled] [ntp-active-server] [assignment-method]' displays the state, including the currently active NTP server. The ntp object is system-managed and cannot be manually added or deleted. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Authentication itself needs an ntp-key, referenced from a server via 'set ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <id>'.

NTP keys are managed with 'add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <value> key-value <value> [is-trusted <value>]', plus matching set/show/delete forms. key-type, the hash algorithm for NTP message digest computation, accepts sha-1, aes-cmac, sha-256 and md5; there is no default. key-id is a number in the range 1..65534. key-value is a string of length 8..40 characters. is-trusted marks the key as a trusted NTP key and takes true/false, defaulting to false. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: 'add ntp-key-2 is-trusted true key-type sha-1 key-value Infinera'.

Yes. The ntp-server origin attribute is exactly for this: a user can convert a DHCP configured NTP entry into a manually configured one by changing this attribute. Run 'set ntp-server-<ip-address> origin manual'. origin takes dhcp (address assigned to this system by a DHCP server) or manual (address manually configured), and the default is manual. Other ntp-server attributes are auth-key-id (uint32 or not-applicable, default not-applicable), label (0..256 chars), admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock) and alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed); show adds oper-state and avail-state. The ip-address key may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or DNS domain name. At the ntp level, assignment-method (manual, dhcp, both; default both) controls which configured values the system uses.

Use 'show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>', for example 'show ntp-server-status-172.19.13.218'. The reach attribute is the reachability indicator: it is an 8-bit shift register with the most recent probe in the 2^0 position, and a value of 377 means all the recent probes have been answered. Supporting attributes are when (seconds elapsed since the last packet was received), poll (polling interval in seconds), delay (path delay to the server in ms), offset (clock offset to the peer in ms), jitter (path jitter in ms), stratum of the remote peer, refid (reference clock type or address), type (local, unicast, multicast or broadcast), auth-status (ok, yes, bad or none, default none) and condition (for example sys.peer, reject, candidate). Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

'restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]' takes type cold, warm or shutdown. cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting; the system regains connectivity within five minutes. A cold reboot of an XMM4 is not service affecting but visibility is lost. warm reboots only the processor of the CHM6, UCM4, etc. and is non service affecting, again regaining connectivity within five minutes; a warm reboot of an XMM4 loses visibility for 3 minutes. shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. If you do not give <type>, the default is warm; if you do not give <resource-id>, the active controller card is restarted. Cards support cold/warm/shutdown, card sub-components cold/warm, toms cold only, and not all cards support all types. Confirmation is required unless -f is given.

Because set-time is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled. If NTP is running the node takes its time from the server and the manual set is rejected; check with 'show clock time-source' (ntp or manual, default manual) and disable NTP with 'set ntp ntp-enabled false' if you really need to set it by hand. The syntax is 'set-time [new-time=]<value>' in Operational mode, with the value in a format derived from ISO 8601 combining date and time, for example 'set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z' where Z is UTC. A non-UTC timezone is allowed by supplying +/-hh:mm instead of Z, for example 'set-time 2021-04-01T18:46:44+03:00'. Retrieve the current time with the 'time' command, which reports it in the system configured timezone rather than the timezone used in set-time.

Yes, 'status equipment'. The Equipment dashboard summarises all equipment in the system with relevant details such as temperature sensors and power values, listing chassis, the cards per chassis and their subtype, the toms per card, and generic status: presence or absence, oper-state and alarms. The default scope is the entire network element. For large NEs you can filter per chassis by giving the chassis id, for example 'status equipment 5'; only existing chassis ids are accepted and wildcards are not supported, so you get either all chassis or exactly one. Output uses symbols: a check for oper-state enabled/admin-state unlocked/no alarms, a cross for oper-state disabled, and a padlock for admin-state lock. Syntax is 'status [[dashboard=]<system | equipment | L0-oxcon | L0-ocm | L1-traffic>] [[filter=]<value>]', Operational mode.

Use 'clear [-f] system [[action=]<value>] [[restart-behavior=]<value>] [type=]<value> [[target=]<value>]'. type is the mode: factory-reset resets the system or a particular equipment to factory configuration, stopping target traffic services and removing the respective files and user configurations, which may imply loss of connectivity; full-wipe cleans the entire system and reinstalls the SW on controller and line-cards, and needs a base software reinstall from ONIE to recover; inactive clears the inactive software partition. restart-behavior is a standard restart (default) or shutdown, where the system does not restart afterwards. target is the whole system or a specific chassis or card AID; with no target the entire system is cleared. Limits: factory-reset does not take effect on 1830 GX G30 Optical Carrier-Cards (OCC2T, OCC2E) but is supported on the G30 controller card (FRCU), and factory-reset with the shutdown option is not supported on L0 cards. For a simple database wipe use 'clear database'. Example: 'clear system factory-reset shutdown'.

Just type 'time'. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. It prints the system's time in combined ISO 8601 date-and-time form with the offset, for example 2020-06-29T22:29:37+00:00, based on the system configured timezone. If you want the surrounding detail instead, 'show clock' returns current-time, universal-time, timezone, uptime, uptime-seconds, time-source, DST-active and last-time-jump.

The 'uptime' command displays the system uptime and load average, for example: '21:24:09 up 41 days, 15:56, 1 user, load average: 0.10, 0.35, 0.39'. The load average, also called average system load, indicates whether there are multiple tasks queued on the system (on the card). Whether it is high or low depends on the number of cores the system has, how many CPUs are integrated into the card, and the load average number itself. The stated rule of thumb: a load average value is considered high when it is greater than the number of CPUs on the card. The command takes no parameters and runs in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. The command is 'manual-switchover [-f] [resource=]<value>' in Operational mode, where resource is the AID of the object to be switched, for example 'manual-switchover card-1-3' on a 1830 GX G42, 'manual-switchover card-1-5' on a G32, or 'manual-switchover card-1-12' on a G34c. It prompts: 'Controller will switchover and connection to the management interface will be lost. Do you want to continue? [y/n]'. You confirm at that prompt to proceed, or pass -f to force it without confirmation. So expect to lose the management connection and reconnect to the newly active controller. For the full procedure see the 1830 GX Software Management Procedures Guide.

'show protection' displays the node's protection container. It is a show-only command with no parameters, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For detail below it, use 'show protection-group-<name>' for group state (pg-state, pg-request, switching-mode, reversion-mode, hold-off-timer, wtr-timer, remaining-wtr, last-switch-trigger, working-pu, protection-pu) and 'show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name>' for the per-member state and role.

On protection-group, switching-mode takes unidirectional or bidirectional and defaults to unidirectional. wtr-timer is the trigger clearance soaking time before reverting to the working protection unit, measured and set in 1-second steps, with a range of 60..720 seconds and a default of 300; it is only applicable in revertive mode, and reversion-mode itself defaults to non-revertive (values revertive, non-revertive), so you must set reversion-mode revertive for the WTR timer to matter. The read-only remaining-wtr shows the time left, range 0..720 seconds, again only in revertive mode. The related hold-off-timer is the switching trigger soaking time before switching, in 1-millisecond steps, range 0..10000 ms, default 0. All are set with 'add/set protection-group-<name> ...'.

Use the operating command 'protection-switch [-f] [operation-type=]<value> [switch-target=]<value> [protection-group=]<value>' in Operational mode. operation-type takes force, lockout, manual or release; switch-target is the target of the switch and is not needed for the release and lockout operations. For example: 'protection-switch protection-group-test operation-type=force switch-target=protection'. Pass -f to skip confirmation. Equivalently the group's pg-request attribute can be set with 'set protection-group-<name> pg-request forced-to-protection'; pg-request accepts clear (default), manual-to-working, manual-to-protection, forced-to-working, forced-to-protection, protection-lockout and exercise (applicable only for bidirectional SNCP). The resulting condition appears in pg-state as forced-to-protection.

Read the state attribute of the protection units: 'show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name> [AID] [transport-entity] [state] [role] [alarm-report-control] [label]'. state takes active, standby, available or unknown, so the member reporting active is the one carrying traffic. role tells you which member is which, taking working or protection. transport-entity gives the instance identifier of the underlying transport entity. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. At group level, 'show protection-group-<name> pg-state last-switch-trigger' tells you why the current selection is in place. Only alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default inhibited) and label are settable on a protection-unit.

Most alarms have both an automatic raise criteria and a clear criteria, but a small subset have no clear criteria and require the user to acknowledge and clear them manually. Clear one with 'clear [-f] alarm [alarm-type=]<value> [[resource=]<value>[,<value>]*]', for example 'clear alarm DBRESTOREFAIL'; -f forces the command without confirmation. To find which of your stuck alarms are eligible, list the inventory entries flagged can-be-cleared-by-user: 'show alarm-inventory can-be-cleared-by-user=true'. Note the restriction: this mechanism applies only to system alarms that are not associated with any particular resource but with the system itself, that is system wide/global alarms. Access is Operational mode.

That is decided by the system wide alarm-reporting-control behavior switch, 'set alarm-control arc-behavior <value>'. It takes leave-alarms, which leaves current alarms in a raised mode when ARC is set to inhibit, or clear-alarms, which clears current alarms when ARC is set to inhibit. The default is leave-alarms, so by default alarms already raised stay up when you inhibit reporting. Change it with 'set alarm-control arc-behavior clear-alarms' and check it with 'show alarm-control'. The same object carries alarm-soaking-behavior (automatic, using the soaking time defined in the FM profile, or no-soak, where certain alarms specified in the FM profile have no soaking time; default automatic). Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Per-object inhibiting is done with the alarm-report-control attribute (allowed/inhibited) on the entity.

Look it up in the alarm inventory, which holds all possible alarm types for the system with static information for each: 'show alarm-inventory-<alarm-type> [resource-type] [alarm-category] [alarm-type-description] [corrective-action] [default-severity] [service-affecting]', for example 'show alarm-inventory-TIM' or 'show alarm-inventory-MSIM'. alarm-type-description is the description of the alarm type (string 0..128), and corrective-action is system provided information on how to correct the situation that triggered the alarm (string 0..256). alarm-category is one of communication, facility, equipment, environmental, processing-error, software, quality-of-service or security. default-severity lists the possible defaults (critical, major, minor, warning, not-reported, event), which can differ per resource-type. service-affecting is indeterminate, sa, nsa or sa-nsa.

Yes, that is exactly what alarm-severity-entry is for: it configures the severity for one particular alarm. Use 'set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <value>', for example 'set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor' or 'set alarm-severity-entry-tom/EQPTCOMFAIL severity major'. resource-type is the card or entity type (for example CHM1R, FAN, 1830 GX G31), alarm-type is the abbreviated code (for example ADMIN-LOCK, BERSD), direction is na, ingress or egress, and location is na, near-end or far-end. severity takes critical, event, major, minor, not-reported or warning. Read it back with 'show alarm-severity-entry-...', which also returns service-affecting (indeterminate, sa, nsa, sa-nsa). Press ? after 'set alarm-severity-entity' to list available entities. The object is system-managed and cannot be manually deleted.

alarm-severity-profile sets the severity for a whole profile entry rather than for one resource-type/alarm-type/direction/location combination. Syntax: 'set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <critical|event|major|minor|not-reported|warning>' and 'show alarm-severity-profile'; press ? after 'set alarm-severity-profile' to list available profiles. Example: 'set alarm-severity-profile alarm-severity-entry-trusted-certificate/CERTIFICATE-EXPIRED severity critical'. By contrast alarm-severity-entry is keyed per instance as alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> and also exposes service-affecting on show. Both take the same severity value set, both run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, and both objects are managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted.

Use 'show current-alarms [number-of-alarms] [last-changed]'. number-of-alarms is the count of currently raised alarms, and last-changed is the timestamp of the last change in the current alarm list, covering either a raise or a clear event. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. If you want the count broken down by severity, the system dashboard from the 'status' command reports it, for example '13 current alarms (1 critical, 5 major, 2 not-reported, 5 minor)'. For the alarms themselves use 'show alarms' or 'show alarm-<alarm-id>' with filters.

Look at conditions with the 'get-conditions' command. A condition is an alarm that is not considered current, which happens when the alarm severity is configured as not-reported or not-alarmed, when the alarm is suppressed due to alarm correlation, when it is suppressed due to ARC (alarm reporting control), or when it is suppressed due to AINS. Syntax: 'get-conditions [[direction=]<value>] [[resource=]<value>] [[resource-type=]<value>] [[alarm-type=]<value>] [[location=]<value>] [[AID=]<value>]'. direction takes all, na, ingress or egress and defaults to all; location takes all, na, near-end or far-end and also defaults to all; resource, resource-type, alarm-type and AID have no default. Access is Operational mode.
